CSOs, indigenous peoples, local communities, farmers, pastoralists, women and youth should participate systematically in national reporting, with their contributions reflected in official reports. Community based monitoring, participatory mapping, citizen science, traditional knowledge and participatory data collection can strengthen national datasets and improve transparency. Practical mechanisms are needed to integrate this information into reporting. Third, reporting systems must be accessible and user-friendly. Simplified platforms, multilingual interfaces, accessible digital tools, and guidance adapted to local contexts should facilitate participation rather than create barriers. Fourth, capacity building must extend beyond national institutions. Grassroots organizations and communities need support in technical skills, data management, geospatial methods, digital literacy and participatory monitoring to engage effectively in reporting. Fifth, transparency and open access are essential. National reports, data sets and methodologies should be publicly accessible, accompanied by simplified communication products that make results understandable and useful to wider audiences. Sixth, reporting must balance scientific rigor with practical realities. Quantitative indicators should be complemented by qualitative evidence, case studies and local experiences that capture the social dimensions of restoration, drought resilience and sustainable land management. Finally, reporting must be gender responsive and strengthen science policy processes. This requires sex disaggregated data, gender responsive indicators and meaningful participation of women, including from indigenous peoples and local communities. Reporting must measure what is happening on the ground, but it also must help improve what happens on the ground. We end this intervention by expressing our deep concern over the exclusion of gender, civil society participation and synergies from the COP agenda.
